article.kick: Yom Tov · Shevi'i V'acharon Shel Pesach
article.body:

In the year תרכ”ה )1865(, the Rebbe Maharash was sitting at the Yom Tov table with his family. Four- year-old (future Rebbe) Rashab asked, “Why is the last day of Pesach a Yom Tov?” His ten- year-old sister, Devorah Leah, answered, “The Yidden have been careful not to eat chametz for seven days straight! So, we make a Yom Tov to celebrate our fulfillment of this mitzvah.” Smiling, the Rebbe Maharash complimented his daughter, “You have a good head!”

When the Rebbe Maharash went with his children to visit his father, the Tzemach Tzedek, he repeated the conversation. The Tzemach Tzedek agreed that Devorah Leah gave a good, logical answer. He then called the children closer, and told them another answer. “Today is called ‘ּפֶסַַח ׁשֶל אַחֲרֹון—The Last Day of Pesach’ because we’ve finished the avodah of Pesach, when Hashem redeemed us from Golus Mitzrayim. Acharon shel Pesach celebrates Hashem redeeming us from this final Golus.”

On the night of Acharon shel Pesach תרס"ו )1906(, the Rebbe Rashab heard his granddaughters arguing. One girl said that Acharon shel Pesach is a regular Yom Tov, but young Chaya Mushka (our Rebbetzin) said: “No, it’s not! The proof is that we don’t say shehecheyanu on Acharon shel Pesach [showing that it’s different from all other Yomim Tovim]!”

When the Rebbe Rashab heard that, he was reminded of the story with his sister Devorah Leah.

On Shvi’i and Acharon shel Pesach, we don’t say the bracha of שֶׁהֶחֱיָנּו, unlike any other Yom Tov. Do you know why? The simple answer is because the whole Pesach is one long Yom Tov, so the last days are not “new”. But there is also a deeper answer. You’ll never guess who figured it out. It was our rebbetzin, Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka, when she was only five years old!

When’s the latest you’ve ever gone to sleep? If you’re old enough, there might be times when you stay up all night! That’s because there are a few times throughout the year when we have the minhag not to go to sleep. One of those nights is Shvi’i shel Pesach. Do you know why? Let’s think of what happened on the first Shvi’i shel Pesach: The Yidden left Mitzrayim on Tes-Vov Nissan, and then, on Chof-Alef Nissan (Shvi’i shel Pesach), Hashem made the wondrous neis of Kri’as Yam Suf! The Torah teaches us that Kri’as Yam Suf wasn’t just a gashmiyus neis of water splitting. It was also a time of incredible giluy Elokus. In fact, simple maidservants saw deeper levels of Elokus there than even the great navi Yechezkel saw with nevu’a years later! Because the ruchniyus energy of a Yom Tov happens again each year (and on an even greater level than before!), we want to be awake for these special giluyim. Minhag Chabad is to stay up all night until dawn. What do we do all night? We learn Torah— especially Chassidus. The Frierdiker Rebbe began staying up all night when he was nine years old.

Menachem, vol. 43, pp. 201–202, 243–250; Likkutei Sichos,

vol. 22, pp. 30–38; Toras Menachem, vol. 33, pp. 336–341.

That’s right: Until now, we were very careful about gebroks. But on Acharon shel Pesach, that all changes. Now, we specifically wet our matzah. Do you know why?

Chametz represents ga’ava. It rises and is full of air, like a person full of pride. Matzah is flat and low, which represents being humble. On Pesach, we work very hard to have zero traces of ga’ava. So, we have zero chametz—not even gebroks, which is just a tiny chance of chametz.

But pride is not always bad. We’re supposed to be proud of who we are. Aren’t you proud to be a chayol in Hashem’s Army? As long as we remember that everything comes from Hashem, we can and should be proud.

So, once we’ve practiced being humble for the whole week of Pesach, we can start having ga’ava again—the right kind. On Acharon shel Pesach, we bring in a little bit of pride by eating gebroks. (And on Shavuos, when the avodah of Pesach is complete, we bring actual chametz onto the mizbe’ach!) This way, we can be proud chayolim the whole year while remembering that Hashem is the One in control!

Our Rebbe explained how the two stories are connected:

According to Devorah Leah, this Yom Tov celebrates not eating chametz, which is connected to our Yetzer Hara and Golus—so it is similar to other Yomim Tovim. However, our Rebbetzin’s argument is similar to the Tzemach Tzedek’s answer, connecting Acharon shel Pesach to the Geulah. It’s different from all other Yomim Tovim.

When the end of Pesach comes—after we’ve worked hard for a whole week to leave Golus— but Moshiach still isn’t here yet, it’s very painful, so we don’t say shehecheyanu. But when we celebrate Acharon shel Pesach with simcha and emuna, it makes it happen for real!

How many cups of wine (or grape juice) do Chassidim drink that are connected specifically to Pesach? The answer is 12! Four at each Seder night, and another four at Moshiach’s Seuda.

Moshiach’s Seuda was started by the Baal Shem Tov. Our Rebbeim explain that a ray of Moshiach’s energy shines during this time. We tap into it with a special seuda! Since Moshiach will affect even (and especially!) our gashmiyus world, we use gashmiyus to celebrate. We eat matzah and, as the Rebbe Rashab added, we drink four cups of wine.

Ever wonder why there’s no maror at Moshiach’s Seudah? That’s because we are focused on Geulah, when there will be no more sadness or pain. We can serve Hashem with pure simcha!

Therefore, when drinking the wine (which brings simcha and geshmak), be sure to think about the Geulah—may it happen immediately!
